name: Triangle from Back
description: Learn Triangle from Back in BJJ. Step-by-step setup from Harness to Rear Triangle control. Master the leg threading sequence and chain attacks.
overview:
The Triangle from Back is an advanced submission setup that transitions from the harness (seat belt) back control position into a rear triangle configuration. Rather than attacking the neck directly with a rear naked choke, the practitioner threads one leg over the opponent's shoulder and locks a figure-four triangle around the head and one arm, establishing the Rear Triangle control position. This technique exploits a common defensive pattern where the opponent strips the choking arm or tucks their chin aggressively against the rear naked choke, opening the space needed to insert the leg over the shoulder.

Strategically, the Triangle from Back is a high-level chain attack that punishes opponents who commit both hands to defending the rear naked choke. When the opponent pulls the choking arm below chin level with a two-on-one grip, their shoulder opens and the top player can swing the leg over the trapped shoulder to establish the triangle. The technique requires excellent hip dexterity and the ability to maintain back control while transitioning leg position, making it a technique that separates intermediate from advanced practitioners. Once the rear triangle is locked, the bottom player faces a severe positional disadvantage with multiple submission threats including the triangle choke squeeze, armbar on the trapped arm, and wrist locks.

The Triangle from Back serves as a critical branch in the back attack decision tree. When opponents develop strong rear naked choke defense, this option forces them to choose between defending the choke and exposing the triangle entry, creating the kind of offensive dilemma that elite back attackers rely on to finish matches.
conditions: Harness grip established with chest-to-back connection
Opponent defending rear naked choke with two-on-one grip, creating shoulder gap
At least one hook inserted for lower body control
Far-side arm controlled or pinned to prevent blocking the leg thread

attacker.name: Triangle from Back Attacker
attacker.description: How to execute Triangle from Back in BJJ. Attacking perspective with setup, execution steps, and counters.
attacker.overview:
The Triangle from Back is an advanced submission setup that transitions from the harness (seat belt) back control position into a rear triangle configuration. Rather than attacking the neck directly with a rear naked choke, the practitioner threads one leg over the opponent's shoulder and locks a figure-four triangle around the head and one arm, establishing the Rear Triangle control position. This technique exploits a common defensive pattern where the opponent strips the choking arm or tucks their chin aggressively against the rear naked choke, opening the space needed to insert the leg over the shoulder.

Strategically, the Triangle from Back is a high-level chain attack that punishes opponents who commit both hands to defending the rear naked choke. When the opponent pulls the choking arm below chin level with a two-on-one grip, their shoulder opens and the top player can swing the leg over the trapped shoulder to establish the triangle. The technique requires excellent hip dexterity and the ability to maintain back control while transitioning leg position, making it a technique that separates intermediate from advanced practitioners. key_principles: Attack the triangle when the opponent commits both hands to defending the choking arm, creating the shoulder opening needed for leg insertion
Maintain chest-to-back connection throughout the transition to prevent the opponent from turning and escaping during the leg switch
Use the non-choking arm to control the opponent's far wrist or bicep, preventing them from blocking the incoming leg
Thread the leg over the shoulder in a smooth arc, keeping the knee tight to the opponent's neck to prevent them from ducking under
Lock the figure-four triangle configuration immediately after the leg clears the shoulder, before the opponent can posture or strip the leg
Keep hooks active during the transition phase to prevent the opponent from spinning out or creating distance while the leg is being threaded
setup_requirements: Harness (seat belt) grip established with chest-to-back connection from back control
Opponent is actively defending the rear naked choke with both hands, pulling the choking arm below their chin and creating a shoulder gap
At least one hook inserted to maintain lower body control during the leg threading transition
Sufficient hip mobility to swing the leg over the opponent's shoulder while maintaining back position
Control of the opponent's far-side arm or wrist to prevent them from blocking the incoming leg

execution_steps.description: From harness position with seat belt grip established, begin working the choking arm toward the neck to force the opponent to commit both hands to defending. Drive the choking forearm toward the neck while maintaining chest pressure on their back.

Recognize when the opponent pulls your choking arm down with a strong two-on-one grip, tucking their chin and committing both hands low. This creates the opening above the defending shoulder that the triangle leg will thread through.

Release the underhook arm from the harness and use it to control the opponent's far-side wrist or bicep. Pin this arm against their body to prevent them from posting or blocking your incoming leg. Maintain the choking arm position as a frame reference.

Remove the hook on the same side as your choking arm by pulling your foot out from inside their thigh. Bring the knee up toward your chest to load the leg for the over-the-shoulder thread. Keep the opposite hook deep to prevent the opponent from spinning away.

execution_steps.action: Thread the leg over the shoulder
execution_steps.description: Swing the freed leg in an arc over the opponent's shoulder on the choking arm side. The back of your knee should land tight against the side of their neck with your shin crossing their chest or collarbone. Keep the motion fluid and committed to prevent them from catching the leg mid-transition.

Once the leg is over the shoulder, angle the knee downward to trap their head and one arm inside the triangle. The opponent's defending arm that was fighting the choke is now trapped between your leg and their own neck, creating the classic triangle configuration from the back.

Bring your other leg up and hook the ankle of your top leg behind the knee of the bottom leg to establish the figure-four lock. Squeeze your knees together to tighten the triangle around the opponent's neck and trapped arm, consolidating the Rear Triangle control position.

Once the figure-four is locked, adjust your hip angle to maximize choking pressure. Pull the opponent's trapped arm across their body to tighten the strangle. Use your free hand to control their posture or set up additional submission threats from the secured Rear Triangle position.

common_counters.counter: Opponent tucks chin and pulls their shoulder down to block the leg from threading over, closing the gap above the shoulder
common_counters.your_response: Maintain choke pressure to keep them reacting with both hands low, then use your controlling arm to pry the shoulder open by pushing on their elbow or use a wrist-peel to create the gap

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips the threading leg as it comes over the shoulder by grabbing the ankle or shin and pushing it away before the triangle locks
common_counters.your_response: If the leg is intercepted, immediately re-attack the rear naked choke while the opponent has released their defensive grip to fight the leg. The choke-to-triangle-to-choke chain creates a constant dilemma

common_counters.counter: Opponent turns into you during the transition when the hook is withdrawn, attempting to recover guard or escape to half guard
common_counters.your_response: Use the remaining hook and your underhook control to prevent the turn. If they partially turn, adapt by transitioning to a front triangle or switch to an armbar setup using the exposed arm

common_counters.counter: Opponent postures up explosively and stacks forward when they feel the leg coming over, attempting to create distance and prevent the lock
common_counters.your_response: Follow with your hips and maintain the chest-to-back connection. Their forward posture actually makes it easier to close the triangle once the leg is over since their head drops forward into the triangle gap

common_errors.error: Releasing chest-to-back connection while threading the leg, creating space between bodies
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes back control entirely by turning into guard or standing up during the momentary gap in control
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant chest pressure throughout the transition by keeping hips close and using the remaining hook to anchor your lower body to the opponent

common_errors.error: Attempting the triangle without first forcing the opponent to commit both hands to choke defense
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses their free hand to block the incoming leg or to strip the hook, preventing the triangle from being established
common_errors.correction: Always threaten the rear naked choke first and wait for the two-on-one defensive reaction before initiating the leg thread

common_errors.error: Threading the leg too slowly or hesitating mid-arc over the shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Opponent catches the leg during transition, strips it, and may escape to turtle or half guard while you have compromised hook control
common_errors.correction: Commit to the leg thread as a single fluid motion once initiated. Practice the arc repeatedly in drilling to build the speed and confidence needed

common_errors.error: Removing both hooks simultaneously to free the leg instead of keeping one hook active
common_errors.consequence: Complete loss of lower body control allows opponent to spin, sit up, or scramble free of the back position entirely
common_errors.correction: Only remove one hook at a time. Keep the opposite hook deep and active throughout the entire transition to maintain lower body control

common_errors.error: Failing to lock the figure-four immediately after the leg clears the shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Opponent pushes the loose leg off their shoulder and returns to defending the standard back control before the triangle is secured
common_errors.correction: Train to lock the figure-four as a reflex the moment the leg clears. The lock must happen within 2-3 seconds or the window closes

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control the opponent's far arm during the transition phase
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses their free hand to post on the mat and create a frame that prevents the leg from clearing the shoulder or blocks the triangle lock
common_errors.correction: Pin the far-side wrist or bicep with your underhook hand before initiating the leg thread to eliminate their ability to block

training_progressions.description: Practice the isolated motion of threading the leg over a compliant partner's shoulder from back control. Focus on hip dexterity, maintaining chest connection, and the arc of the leg. Drill the figure-four lock from various angles until the locking motion becomes automatic. No resistance from partner.

Partner provides light choke defense with two-on-one grip. Practice reading the defensive commitment and timing the transition from choke threat to triangle entry. Work the full sequence from choke threat through triangle lock with partner providing realistic but controlled defensive reactions.

Partner provides medium resistance including attempting to block the leg, turn in, or strip hooks during the transition. Practice adapting mid-technique: if triangle is blocked, return to choke; if opponent turns, switch to armbar. Develop the ability to flow between attacks based on defensive responses.

Incorporate triangle from back into live rolling from back control positions. Start rounds from harness position and work to identify the correct timing window against fully resisting opponents. Track success rate and identify which defensive patterns trigger the triangle entry most reliably.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Triangle from Back?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to transition from harness (seat belt) back control into the Rear Triangle control position by threading one leg over the opponent's shoulder and locking a figure-four around their head and one trapped arm. This establishes a dominant submission control position with multiple finishing options including the triangle choke squeeze and armbar on the trapped arm.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive reaction from your opponent creates the optimal window to initiate the triangle entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal window opens when the opponent commits both hands to a two-on-one grip on your choking arm, pulling it below their chin to defend the rear naked choke. This two-handed commitment creates an undefended gap above the shoulder on the choking side and removes their ability to block the incoming leg. Without this commitment, the opponent can use their free hand to intercept the leg thread.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent posts their far hand on the mat as you begin threading the leg - how do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: You should have controlled the far-side arm before initiating the leg thread. If they post despite your control, use your underhook arm to strip their posting hand by cupping their wrist and pulling it back to their body. If you cannot strip the post, abort the triangle attempt and re-attack the rear naked choke while their hand is occupied posting rather than defending the neck. Then re-attempt the triangle when they return both hands to choke defense.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most critical hip movement during the leg threading phase of this technique?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The critical hip movement is a lateral hip shift away from the leg you are threading, combined with a slight upward hip elevation. This creates the clearance needed to swing the leg over the shoulder in a smooth arc. Without this hip adjustment, the leg gets caught on the opponent's shoulder or lacks the range of motion to clear. Think of it as shifting your hips to create space for the leg like opening a gate rather than trying to force the leg through a tight gap.

knowledge_assessment.question: Which grips must you maintain throughout the entire transition from harness to rear triangle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: You must maintain at least one point of upper body control at all times. The choking arm stays in contact with the opponent's upper chest or neck area as a reference frame, while the underhook arm transitions from the harness to far-arm control. Additionally, the non-threading hook must stay deep in the opponent's thigh throughout. At no point should all contact points be released simultaneously, as this creates the gap the opponent needs to escape.

knowledge_assessment.question: What direction of force should the threading leg travel, and why is this specific arc important?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The threading leg travels in an upward arc from behind the opponent, over the shoulder, and then downward in front of the neck. The arc must be tight to the opponent's head and shoulder rather than wide and looping. A wide arc gives the opponent time to intercept the leg and creates distance between your chest and their back. A tight arc keeps the knee close to their neck, minimizes transition time, and maintains chest-to-back pressure throughout the movement.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent defends the triangle by tucking their shoulder and pulling their arm back tight to their body - what chain attack do you use?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the opponent pulls their shoulder tight to prevent the leg from clearing, immediately return to the rear naked choke attack. Their defensive posture of pulling the shoulder down typically opens the neck by creating slack in their chin tuck. This choke-to-triangle-to-choke cycle is the fundamental chain: defending one attack opens the other. After they re-commit to choke defense, the triangle window opens again. This constant oscillation between threats is what makes elite back attackers so dangerous.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the common failure points that cause the triangle to fail even after the leg successfully clears the shoulder?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most common failure after clearing the shoulder is taking too long to lock the figure-four, giving the opponent time to push the loose leg off. Second is failing to trap the correct arm inside the triangle, which eliminates choking pressure. Third is not adjusting hip angle after locking, resulting in a loose triangle that the opponent can posture out of. Fourth is neglecting to pull the trapped arm across the body, which is necessary to tighten the strangle and prevent the opponent from creating defensive frames inside the triangle.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the Triangle from Back differ from the Triangle Choke Back entry, and when would you choose one over the other?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Triangle from Back is initiated from standard harness control and involves threading a leg over the opponent's shoulder in response to choke defense. The Triangle Choke Back typically involves transitioning from body triangle control with a different mechanical entry. Choose Triangle from Back when you have harness grip and the opponent defends the rear naked choke with both hands. Choose the body triangle variant when you already have body triangle established and want to transition your leg control into a triangle without giving up the body lock first.

knowledge_assessment.question: What entry requirements must exist before you can safely attempt the Triangle from Back without risking loss of position?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Five conditions must be met: (1) secure harness grip with chest-to-back connection, (2) at least one hook inserted for lower body control, (3) opponent committed to two-handed choke defense creating the shoulder opening, (4) control of the far-side arm to prevent blocking, and (5) sufficient space above the shoulder for the leg to thread through. Attempting without these conditions leads to failed entries where you lose hooks, give up back control, or get stuck mid-transition in a compromised position.

attacker.safety_considerations: The Triangle from Back involves significant neck compression and cervical spine stress on the bottom player once the rear triangle is locked. Training partners must tap early when the triangle tightens around the neck, as the choking pressure from a rear triangle can cause unconsciousness rapidly due to bilateral carotid compression. The threading motion can also strain the top player's hip flexors and groin if forced without adequate flexibility. During drilling, practice the leg thread at controlled speed and avoid cranking the triangle lock aggressively. Partners with neck injuries or cervical disc issues should avoid being placed in the bottom position. Always establish clear tap signals before drilling this technique, and release immediately upon any tap or verbal submission.

defender.name: Triangle from Back Defender
defender.description: How to defend against Triangle from Back in BJJ. Recognition cues, defensive options, and escape strategies.
defender.overview:
Defending the Triangle from Back requires acute awareness of the attacker's setup sequence and the ability to disrupt their leg threading before the figure-four locks. As the defender, you are already in a compromised position with your back taken, and the triangle entry compounds your problems by threatening to trap one arm inside the leg configuration, drastically reducing your defensive options. The key defensive window exists during the transition phase when the attacker withdraws one hook to thread the leg over your shoulder. This momentary reduction in lower body control is your best opportunity to turn, create angles, or escape before the triangle consolidates.

The defensive priority hierarchy is clear: first, prevent the leg from clearing the shoulder entirely by keeping your shoulders tight and denying the gap the attacker needs. Second, if the leg does clear, fight the figure-four lock by controlling the attacker's ankle or pushing the leg off before it connects to the other knee. Third, if the triangle locks, immediately address the trapped arm and work systematic escapes before the choking pressure becomes critical. Understanding that the triangle entry is triggered by your own two-handed choke defense is essential. By varying your defensive hand positioning and not over-committing both hands to the choking arm, you can reduce the frequency of triangle attempts while still maintaining viable choke defense.

Successful defense against this technique demands a balance between defending the rear naked choke and denying the triangle entry. Experienced defenders learn to keep one hand fighting the choke while the other monitors the attacker's hip and leg movement, ready to block any leg threading attempt. This split-attention defensive posture is more demanding but eliminates the binary choice between choke defense and triangle vulnerability that the attacker is trying to exploit.
key_principles: Keep shoulders tight and chin tucked to deny the gap above the shoulder that the attacker needs to thread the leg through
Avoid committing both hands fully to choke defense simultaneously, as this creates the exact opening the triangle entry requires
Monitor the attacker's hip movement and hook withdrawal with tactile awareness, as these are the earliest indicators of the triangle attempt
When the attacker withdraws a hook to begin the leg thread, immediately turn toward the opening to disrupt the transition and recover guard
If the leg clears the shoulder, fight the figure-four lock aggressively before it tightens by controlling the attacker's ankle and pushing the leg off your shoulder
Maintain at least one hand near your shoulder line rather than both hands low on the choking arm, creating a ready block against the incoming leg
recognition_cues: Attacker removes one hook from your thigh while maintaining the harness grip, indicating they are loading the leg for the over-shoulder thread
You feel the attacker's hips shift laterally away from one side, creating the clearance needed to swing the leg in an arc over your shoulder
The attacker's underhook arm releases from the harness and moves to control your far-side wrist or bicep, pinning your arm to prevent you from blocking the incoming leg
Increased upward pressure from the choking arm as the attacker uses it as a frame reference while repositioning their leg, combined with a change in their breathing rhythm indicating effort

defensive_options.action: Shoulder shrug and chin tuck defense - raise the shoulder on the threading side while tucking your chin tight, closing the gap the leg needs to clear
defensive_options.when_to_use: At the earliest recognition that the attacker is withdrawing a hook and beginning the leg threading motion, before the leg reaches the shoulder
defensive_options.if_successful: The attacker's leg cannot clear the shoulder and they must either abandon the triangle attempt and re-establish their hook, returning to standard harness control
defensive_options.risk: If you over-commit the shoulder shrug, you may temporarily reduce your choke defense on that side, giving the attacker a brief window to advance the rear naked choke

defensive_options.action: Turn into the opening - when you feel the hook withdraw, immediately hip escape and turn your body toward the side where the hook was removed to face the attacker
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the transition window when one hook is removed and the attacker has reduced lower body control, before the leg begins its arc over the shoulder
defensive_options.if_successful: You escape the back position entirely and recover to half guard or closed guard by turning to face your opponent before they can re-establish back control
defensive_options.risk: If the turn is too slow or the remaining hook prevents full rotation, you end up in a worse position with the attacker able to transition to a mounted triangle or front-facing control

defensive_options.action: Ankle strip and leg push - grab the attacker's threading leg at the ankle or shin as it comes over the shoulder and push it back over before the figure-four locks
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the leg has already cleared the shoulder but the figure-four has not yet been locked, during the 2-3 second window before the triangle consolidates
defensive_options.if_successful: The triangle is prevented from locking and the attacker must retract the leg, returning to harness position with potentially compromised hook placement
defensive_options.risk: By releasing your grip on the choking arm to fight the leg, you expose your neck to the rear naked choke if the attacker quickly re-attacks rather than pursuing the triangle

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one arm extraction - if the triangle locks with your arm trapped, immediately grip your own wrist and work to pull the trapped arm across your centerline and out of the triangle
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the figure-four is locked and one arm is trapped inside the triangle, as the first priority escape action before the choke tightens fully
defensive_options.if_successful: Extracting the arm removes the mechanical wedge that makes the triangle effective as a choke, dramatically reducing finishing pressure and opening escape pathways
defensive_options.risk: The extraction attempt may fail if the attacker squeezes knees together to prevent arm removal, and the effort expended during failed extraction accelerates fatigue under choking pressure

favorable_outcomes.how: Block the triangle entry by keeping shoulders tight and denying the gap, or strip the leg before the figure-four locks. Maintain two-on-one control on the choking arm while using your far-side elbow to block leg threading attempts. The attacker returns to standard harness position where you resume normal back escape sequences.

Exploit the transition window when the attacker removes a hook to thread the leg. Immediately hip escape and turn toward the opening to face the attacker. Use the reduced lower body control to create enough rotation to recover half guard before the attacker can re-establish hooks or complete the triangle. This requires committed timing and willingness to accept the momentary risk of turning.

common_errors.error: Committing both hands low on the choking arm in a static two-on-one grip without monitoring the attacker's leg and hip movement
common_errors.consequence: Creates the exact shoulder opening the attacker needs to thread the triangle leg, and leaves no hand available to block the incoming leg when it arrives
common_errors.correction: Keep one hand fighting the choking arm while positioning the other hand near your shoulder line, ready to block leg threading attempts. Alternate which hand fights the choke to maintain awareness of both threats.

common_errors.error: Freezing when the leg begins to come over the shoulder instead of immediately fighting to push it off
common_errors.consequence: The 2-3 second window to prevent the figure-four lock closes quickly, and hesitation allows the attacker to complete the triangle unopposed
common_errors.correction: Train an automatic response to any leg contact on your shoulder: immediately grab the ankle or shin and push it back over. This must be a reflex developed through repetitive drilling, not a conscious decision made under pressure.

common_errors.error: Attempting to pull the head out of the locked triangle rather than extracting the trapped arm first
common_errors.consequence: Pulling the head drives the trapped shoulder deeper into the neck, actually increasing the choking pressure and accelerating loss of consciousness
common_errors.correction: Always prioritize arm extraction over head escape. The trapped arm is the mechanical component that makes the triangle effective as a blood choke. Remove the arm first, then the head can follow with reduced resistance.

common_errors.error: Panicking and making explosive bridging movements after the triangle locks without a technical escape plan
common_errors.consequence: Burns energy rapidly under choking pressure, accelerates oxygen depletion, and the uncontrolled movement may help the attacker adjust their angle for a tighter finish
common_errors.correction: Stay calm, protect the chin, and work methodically through the arm extraction sequence. Controlled technical movement conserves energy and creates more effective escape opportunities than explosive panic responses.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the earliest recognition cue that the Triangle from Back is being attempted?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The earliest cue is feeling the attacker withdraw one hook from your thigh while maintaining the harness grip. This hook removal is the first physical action required before the leg can be threaded over your shoulder. You may also feel their hips shift laterally as they create clearance for the leg arc. Recognizing this moment gives you the maximum defensive window to respond before the leg begins its arc over the shoulder.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why does committing both hands to a two-on-one grip on the choking arm create vulnerability to the triangle entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When both hands grip the choking arm low near your chest, your shoulders naturally open and your far-side arm is occupied and unable to block anything above shoulder level. This creates the exact gap above the shoulder that the attacker needs to thread the triangle leg through. Additionally, with both hands committed low, you have no available hand to intercept or push away the incoming leg. The attacker reads this two-handed commitment as the trigger for the triangle entry specifically because it guarantees an unobstructed path for the leg.

knowledge_assessment.question: The attacker's leg has cleared your shoulder but the figure-four is not yet locked - what is your immediate response?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately grab the attacker's ankle or shin on the leg that just cleared your shoulder and push it back over before they can bring their other leg up to lock the figure-four. You have approximately 2-3 seconds in this window. Use your hand closest to the leg and drive it forcefully back over the shoulder while simultaneously shrugging that shoulder upward to create additional clearance. If you cannot push the leg off, immediately begin working to extract your arm from inside the developing triangle before the lock tightens.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you distribute your defensive attention between the rear naked choke and the triangle entry threat?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Rather than committing both hands entirely to choke defense, maintain a split-attention defensive posture. Keep one hand actively controlling the choking arm wrist with a strong C-grip while positioning the other hand near your shoulder line where it can monitor and block leg threading attempts. Alternate which hand fights the choke every few seconds to prevent the attacker from reading a static pattern. This split approach is more demanding than static two-on-one defense but eliminates the binary vulnerability the attacker is trying to exploit.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent has locked the triangle from the back with your arm trapped - what is your escape priority sequence?
knowledge_assessment.answer: First, protect your chin by tucking it tight to your chest and turning your face toward the non-choking leg side to buy time against the blood choke. Second, grip the attacker's choking leg at the ankle or behind the knee with your free hand to prevent them from tightening further. Third, work to extract your trapped arm by gripping your own wrist and pulling the elbow across your centerline while rotating your shoulder. Fourth, once the arm is free, immediately hip escape and turn toward the side where the triangle pressure is reduced. The sequence is: protect chin, control leg, extract arm, escape position. Skipping steps or reversing the order dramatically reduces escape probability.

training_progressions.description: Partner initiates the triangle from back at 30% speed. Practice identifying the hook withdrawal and hip shift cues, then respond with shoulder shrug and leg blocking. Focus on developing the tactile sensitivity to feel when the triangle is being initiated without needing to see it. Drill 20 repetitions per side with compliant partner.

Partner establishes the rear triangle at various tightness levels. Practice the full arm extraction sequence: chin protection, leg control, arm extraction, positional escape. Work at 50% resistance with partner tightening gradually. Develop comfort under pressure and the ability to work methodically rather than panicking when caught.

Partner alternates between rear naked choke attacks and triangle entries from harness control. Practice maintaining the split-attention defensive posture where one hand fights the choke while the other monitors for the triangle. Build the ability to defend both threats simultaneously without over-committing to either. Partner increases attack speed and variation each session.

Start in harness bottom against fully resisting partners. Track how often you get caught in the triangle versus successfully defending the entry. Identify which defensive habits create the triangle opening and systematically eliminate them. Goal is to force the attacker to abandon triangle attempts and return to standard choke attacks due to consistent defensive interception.

variants_and_adaptations.description: In no-gi, the lack of collar grips makes the rear naked choke the primary threat, which forces stronger two-on-one defense. Thread the leg while controlling the far wrist with an overhook or wrist tie. The slipperier grips in no-gi can make the leg thread faster but the lock harder to maintain.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When training or competing without the gi, especially when opponent has strong rear naked choke defense

variants_and_adaptations.variant_name: Gi-Assisted Rear Triangle with Lapel Feed
variants_and_adaptations.description: Feed the opponent's own lapel across their body and secure it with the far hand before threading the triangle leg. The lapel creates an additional barrier that restricts the opponent's arm movement and prevents them from blocking the incoming leg. The gi material also adds friction that helps maintain the triangle once locked.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In gi training when you have time to establish lapel control before initiating the triangle entry

variants_and_adaptations.description: From body triangle back control, unlock the triangle legs and use a rolling motion to transition the body triangle into a rear triangle around the head and arm. This variant uses the existing leg entanglement as a launching platform rather than threading from scratch.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When you have body triangle established and opponent is defending the choke effectively from that position

position_integration: The Triangle from Back occupies a critical branch point in the back attack decision tree. It functions as the secondary threat that makes the rear naked choke more dangerous by punishing opponents who over-commit to choke defense. Within the modern back attack system, the sequence flows: establish harness, threaten rear naked choke, read opponent's defensive commitment, and branch to triangle entry when both hands defend the choke. The resulting Rear Triangle position offers its own submission tree including triangle squeeze, armbar on the trapped arm, and wrist locks. This creates a multi-layered attack system where each defense opens the next threat, embodying the dilemma-based approach that defines elite back control play. The technique connects the harness position to the triangle control family, bridging two major subsystems of the BJJ knowledge graph.
